attempts.label: DANDI:001530
attempts.paper_title: Contextual gating of whisker-evoked responses by frontal cortex supports flexible decision making
attempts.entry_title: Contextual gating of whisker responses by frontal cortex (Ghaderi et al. 2026)
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main findings held up in this data: inactivating wM2 and ALM during the delay reduced licking, both areas carried the tone context through the delay, whisker responses changed with context, and a lick coding direction separated lick from no-lick trials in wM2. Several single-neuron and population values came out low under the Methods' quiet-trial rule but match the paper under its code's rule. The clustering gave 40 clusters, not 29, and removing cluster 25 did not reliably lower context decoding. Context decoding after the whisker stimulus could not be judged, as the paper does not specify its decoder and two readings disagree. The movement-null-space decoding needs MATLAB toolboxes the agent did not reimplement.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Ghaderi, Crochet and Petersen (2026) on dandiset 001530, which holds 35 Neuropixels sessions in 14 mice performing a delayed context-dependent whisker detection task and 91 optogenetic inactivation sessions. It compares lick probabilities, the effect of inactivating six cortical areas in three task epochs, unit counts, single-neuron and population activity in five areas, context decoding during the delay and after the whisker stimulus, and the clustering of neuronal responses.

outcomes.statement: Mice lick in the response window on 78 +/- 2% of Go-tone Whisker trials and withhold licking in the other trial types (Go-tone No-Whisker 10 +/- 1%, Nogo-tone Whisker 13 +/- 2%, Nogo-tone No-Whisker 1 +/- 0.3%, No-tone Whisker 15 +/- 2%), mean +/- SEM over 35 recording sessions in 14 mice.
outcomes.source: Results, A short-term memory context-dependent whisker detection task, paragraph 1; Figure 1c
outcomes.quote: Mice learned to lick correctly in the reward-predicting trials including the Go-tone and whisker deflection (probability of licking correctly in the reporting window, P(lick) = 78 ± 2%, mean ± standard error of the mean, SEM, n = 35 sessions across N = 14 mice during electrophysiological recordings described later) ... i) Go-tone without whisker deflection, P(lick) = 10 ± 1%; ii) Nogo-tone with whisker deflection, P(lick) = 13 ± 2%; iii) Nogo-tone without whisker deflection, P(lick) = 1 ± 0.3%; and iv) No-tone with whisker deflection, P(lick) = 15 ± 2%
outcomes.notes: Mean +/- SEM over 35 sessions (34 for No-tone Whisker, which one session lacks) of P(lick) on completed trials; Go-tone Whisker 78.18 +/- 2.08, Go-tone No-Whisker 9.90 +/- 1.49, Nogo-tone Whisker 13.08 +/- 1.79, Nogo-tone No-Whisker 1.05 +/- 0.26, No-tone Whisker 14.64 +/- 1.72 percent. All five within tolerance.
deviations: Eleven trials of sub-PG028_ses-20210318T163504 have trial_type 0 and enter no trial type.

outcomes.statement: In quiet Hit trials the whisker deflection is followed by whisker protraction (time to 20% of maximum 58 +/- 8 ms), jaw opening (115 +/- 17 ms) and tongue protrusion (231 +/- 29 ms), and tongue-spout contact at 330 +/- 20 ms.
outcomes.source: Results, A short-term memory context-dependent whisker detection task, paragraph 3; Figure 1f
outcomes.quote: In quiet Hit trials, following the whisker deflection in Go-tone trials, mice rapidly initiated a sequence of movements starting with whisker protraction after ~30 ms (time to 20% max = 58 ± 8 ms), followed by jaw opening (115 ± 17 ms) and then protrusion of the tongue (231 ± 29 ms) (Fig. 1f ) resulting in tongue-spout contact triggering water reward delivery with latency 330 ± 20 ms ( n = 35 sessions during electrophysiological recordings)
outcomes.notes: The lick latency is 330.1 +/- 20.2 ms over 35 sessions, the paper's value. With the maximum over 1.0 to 2.0 s, reading (a) gives whisker 54.4 +/- 4.4, jaw 115.3 +/- 15.3 and tongue 192.4 +/- 18.4 ms (34 sessions each), so the whisker and jaw latencies are within tolerance and the tongue latency, 38.6 ms below 231, is not; reading (b) gives 94.6, 142.9 and 254.6 ms, with only the tongue latency within tolerance. The order whisker, jaw, tongue, spout contact holds under both readings, so both give the criterion's partial case. The means are raised by a few late sessions; the medians over sessions under reading (a) are 50.0, 95.0 and 155.0 ms, and the two PG019 sessions average 315.0 ms for the jaw and 385.0 ms for the tongue. What the answer changed. The first run took the maximum over 1.0 to 1.2 s, as the claims file then said, and gave reading (a) 48.2, 81.5 and 140.0 ms and reading (b) 65.2, 83.3 and 153.6 ms, with only the reading (b) whisker latency within tolerance; it asked whether the window was the paper's, since a crossing at 231 ms cannot occur under a maximum over 200 ms. The reader changed the criterion's window to 1.0 to 2.0 s, the 1 s response window of the Methods (questions/ghaderi-2026.yaml). Under it reading (a) moves two of the three movement latencies into tolerance and reading (b) the tongue latency; the outcome stays partially reproduced. The 1.0 to 1.2 s and 1.0 to 1.5 s windows and the code's mean absolute deviation for the quiet rule (reading a 50.9, 118.0 and 196.0 ms) are shown as variants.
deviations: The latency is the right edge of the first 10 ms bin after 1.0 s that reaches 20% of the maximum, minus 1.0 s (code, PSTHBehavior.m labels bins by their right edge); the paper does not say how the bin is read.
Tongue NaN values are set to 0 before averaging, as Ghaderi2025_Figure1_f_Movements_Hit.m does.
sub-PG064_ses-20220210T183214 has no quiet Hit trial and gives no movement latency.

outcomes.statement: Selecting quiet trials (no whisker or jaw movement in the last 200 ms of the delay) rejects about half of the recorded trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding context from neuronal activity during the delay period, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: This precludes the involvement of orofacial motor or sensory reafference signals from contributing to our decoding analyses, but rejects around half of the recorded trials
outcomes.notes: With the Methods' rule (median absolute deviation) 55.06% of 17,840 completed trials are not quiet (median over sessions 53.33%, range 42.2 to 75.9%); over all 18,976 trials 56.72%. Both readings are just outside 45 to 55% and inside the 30 to 70% band for a partial result. With the code's mean absolute deviation 40.22% of completed trials are rejected. Leaving out the 328 completed trials without video gives 54.22%, within tolerance, but counting them as not quiet is the code's rule (below), so the outcome stays partial.
deviations: Trials without video in their window (343 in all; every session has at least one, and two have many, 243 in sub-PG061_ses-20220212T233813 and 29 in sub-PG038_ses-20210316T152753) fail the rule, as in the code. nwb_findQuietTrial.m (lines 17 to 29, printed in the notebook) takes the threshold with nanmedian and mad(), which drops NaN, and compares the NaN pre-stimulus mean with <=, which fails. Every session has at least one trial with a NaN baseline, so a threshold that kept NaN would reject every trial.

outcomes.statement: Inactivation during the Auditory epoch reduces licking on Go-tone Whisker trials most for A1 (39 +/- 4%), and also for wM2 (33 +/- 6%), wS2 (26 +/- 4%) and wS1 (19 +/- 6%), while ALM and fpS1 inactivation causes no significant decrease.
outcomes.source: Results, Spatiotemporally-specific optogenetic inactivation, paragraph 3; Figure 2b-d
outcomes.quote: For Go-tone Whisker trials, the largest impact of inactivation during the Auditory epoch was found for A1 (39 ± 4% reduction in lick probability, p = 0.0004, n = 17 sessions across N = 9 mice), but significant reductions were also found for inactivation of wM2 (33 ± 6% reduction in lick probability, p = 0.0004, n = 14 sessions across N = 9 mice), wS2 (26 ± 4% reduction in lick probability, p = 0.0004, n = 18 sessions across N = 10 mice) and wS1 (19 ± 6% reduction in lick probability, p = 0.002, n = 16 sessions across N = 10 mice). Importantly, inactivation of either ALM or fpS1 during the Auditory window did not cause any significant decrease in licking during the reporting period.

outcomes.statement: Inactivation during the Delay epoch reduces Go-tone Whisker licking strongly for wM2 (45 +/- 7%) and ALM (32 +/- 5%), more modestly for wS1 (16 +/- 3%), and not significantly for A1, wS2 or fpS1.
outcomes.source: Results, Spatiotemporally-specific optogenetic inactivation, paragraph 3; Figure 2b-d
outcomes.quote: Inactivation during the Delay epoch of Go-tone Whisker trials caused a significant and large reduction in lick probability during the reporting window for wM2 (45 ± 7% reduction in lick probability, p = 0.0004, n = 14 sessions across N = 9 mice) and ALM (32 ± 5% reduction in lick probability, p = 0.0004, n = 9 sessions across N = 8 mice). Inactivation of wS1 also appeared to significantly, albeit more modestly, reduce licking (16 ± 3% reduction in lick probability, p = 0.0004, n = 16 sessions across N = 10 mice). On the other hand, inactivation of A1, wS2 or fpS1 during the Delay epoch did not significantly change lick probability in the reporting window.

outcomes.statement: Inactivation during the Whisker epoch reduces Go-tone Whisker licking for every area except fpS1, most for ALM (52 +/- 4%) and wM2 (48 +/- 4%), then wS1 (38 +/- 3%), wS2 (35 +/- 4%) and A1 (13 +/- 3%).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatiotemporally-specific optogenetic inactivation, paragraph 3; Figure 2b-d
outcomes.quote: Finally, all tested cortical regions, except fpS1, showed a significant reduction in licking probability when inactivation occurred during the Whisker stimulus epoch. The largest effects were found for inactivation of ALM (52 ± 4% reduction in lick probability, p = 0.0003, n = 9 sessions across N = 8 mice) and wM2 (48 ± 4% reduction in lick probability, p = 0.0003, n = 14 sessions across N = 9 mice), followed by wS1 (38 ± 3% reduction in lick probability, p = 0.0003, n = 20 sessions across N = 10 mice), wS2 (35 ± 4% reduction in lick probability, p = 0.0003, n = 18 sessions across N = 10 mice), and A1 (13 ± 3% reduction in lick probability, p = 0.01, n = 17 sessions across N = 9 mice).

outcomes.statement: Inactivation during the auditory window reduces licking significantly more for wM2 than for ALM (33 +/- 6% against 8 +/- 5%).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatiotemporally-specific optogenetic inactivation, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: The effect of inactivation during the auditory window was significantly stronger for wM2 than ALM (reduction in lick probabilities for wM2 = 33 ± 6 % vs ALM = 8 ± 5 %; bootstrap comparison, FDR-corrected, p = 0.009).

statistics.test: bootstrap comparison

outcomes.notes: wM2 33.0 +/- 5.7 (14 sessions) against ALM 7.8 +/- 5.4 (9 sessions). Unpaired bootstrap, 10,000 iterations, reading (a) 9 sessions per area p 0.0024, reading (b) all sessions p 0.0008, 0.0018 after FDR over the 15 area pairs; 1,000 iterations 0.006, 0.002 and 0.005. Both readings give p < 0.05 with wM2 larger. The paper's p 0.009 is not reproduced exactly; the comparison is not in the paper's code.

outcomes.statement: Inactivation has little impact on licking in the trial types other than Go-tone Whisker.
outcomes.source: Results, Spatiotemporally-specific optogenetic inactivation, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: whereas inactivation had little impact upon other trial types
outcomes.notes: Both readings fail. By the bootstrap test (1,000 iterations, FDR within window and trial type) 18 of the 72 changes are significant, where reading (a) allows 7; two changes exceed 13 points (reading b), Go-tone No-Whisker trials in the Auditory window for A1 (-19.0) and wS2 (-15.7). Most significant changes are reductions in licking on Go-tone No-Whisker trials in the Auditory window (8.2 to 19.0 points) and on No-tone Whisker trials in the Whisker window (5.8 to 12.6 points); the smallest significant changes are 1.3 to 1.5 points (Nogo-tone No-Whisker trials, Delay window, wS1 and wS2). The effects are smaller than on Go-tone Whisker trials; the paper's "little impact" is judged here by the reader's two thresholds, which the paper does not give; the Supplementary Fig. 3 legend says only that the effects on the other trial types "were less prominent". Whether the criterion asks more than the paper says is asked of a reader (questions/ghaderi-2026.yaml).
deviations: Both thresholds for "little impact" are the claims file's, not the paper's (the claims file's check marks them as open).

outcomes.statement: Across 35 sessions in 14 mice, 10,294 well-isolated units were recorded in the five areas (A1 780, wS1 1938, wS2 2064, wM2 2749, ALM 2763).
outcomes.source: Results, Spatiotemporal dynamics of neocortical activity, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Altogether, across 35 sessions in 14 mice, we recorded 10,294 well-isolated units located in: i) A1 - 780 units across 14 sessions in 6 mice; ii) wS1 - 1938 units across 24 sessions in 12 mice; iii) wS2 - 2064 units across 24 sessions in 11 mice; iv) wM2 - 2749 units across 18 sessions in 8 mice; and v) ALM - 2763 units across 16 sessions in 6 mice.
outcomes.notes: With the probe area and the CCF filter of Area_list.mat the counts are exactly the paper's (A1 780, wS1 1938, wS2 2064, wM2 2749, ALM 2763, 10,294 in all). Without the CCF filter 12,066 units sit on the five areas' probes, so the counts match only with the filter. Probe sessions and mice per area are the paper's (14 and 6, 24 and 12, 24 and 11, 18 and 8, 16 and 6); for wS2 only 19 sessions in 9 mice keep units after the filter. The files hold no inclusion column; every unit in them is taken as one the paper kept.
deviations: The area of a unit uses Area_list.mat from the Zenodo record, which the dandiset does not hold.

outcomes.statement: In quiet Hit trials, probe-averaged activity changes are largest in A1 in the first 30 ms after the tone, in wM2 and ALM in the last 200 ms of the delay, in wS1 and wS2 in the first 30 ms after the whisker deflection, and in frontal areas 300 to 500 ms after it.
outcomes.source: Results, Spatiotemporal dynamics of neocortical activity, paragraph 2; Figure 3a
outcomes.quote: Averaged across the first 30 ms after the onset of the tone, the auditory cue evoked a fast excitation of neurons primarily in A1. Averaged across the last 200 ms of the delay period, elevated neuronal activity appeared most prominent in frontal areas wM2 and ALM. In the 30 ms following whisker deflection, sensory-evoked activity was primarily localized to wS1 and wS2. The period 300-500 ms after whisker stimulation was used to assess licking-related neuronal activity, which was most prominent in frontal regions.
outcomes.notes: Area means over probes (quiet Hit trials), reading (a) Auditory A1 5.55 Hz (others at most 1.54); Delay wM2 0.70 and ALM 0.35 (A1 0.20); Whisker wS1 6.80 and wS2 5.61; Lick ALM 1.80 and wM2 1.79 (wS2 1.28). Reading (b) and the code's -1 to 0 s baseline give the same ranking, so all four windows hold under both readings.
deviations: Windows are the code's bin selections (Ghaderi2025_Figure3_a_brainmap_activity.m, bins labelled 0.01-0.03, 0.8-1.0, 1.01-1.03 and 1.3-1.5 s); the code uses the -1 to 0 s baseline for every window, shown as a variant.
Only units that pass the CCF filter are averaged, as the code does; the criterion says all cortical neurons on the probe.

outcomes.statement: In grand-average PSTHs of correct quiet trials, firing in wM2 and ALM is elevated during the delay of Go-tone trials compared with Nogo-tone trials, and after the whisker stimulus activity rises in Go-tone Whisker Hit trials compared with all other trial types in wS1, wS2, wM2 and ALM.
outcomes.source: Results, Spatiotemporal dynamics of neocortical activity, paragraph 3; Figure 3b
outcomes.quote: there were two obvious differences comparing Go-tone and Nogo-tone trials: i) there was a prominent elevation in firing rate in wM2 and ALM during the delay period of Go-tone trials compared to Nogo-tone trials; and ii) after the whisker stimulus there was a clear increase of activity in correct Go-tone Whisker trials compared to all other trial types in wS1, wS2, wM2 and ALM
outcomes.notes: (i) holds in wM2 (Wilcoxon over 2,749 neurons, pooled p 0.004, by type p 0.0015) and ALM (2,763 neurons, p 0.009 and 0.008). (ii) over 1.3 to 1.5 s holds in wS1, wM2 and ALM against all four other correct types, and in wS2 against types 2, 3 and 4 but not against No-tone Whisker CR (difference 0.80 Hz, p 0.11), so (ii) fails for one area, the criterion's partial case. Over 1.0 to 1.5 s every comparison holds. With the code's whisker-only quiet rule (i) fails for ALM by type (p 0.055) and (ii) fails for the same wS2 comparison.
deviations: Pooled Go-tone and Nogo-tone conditions pool the trials of the two types.

outcomes.statement: In the last 200 ms of the delay of quiet Hit trials, more wM2 than ALM neurons are up-modulated relative to baseline (16.0% against 14.2%, p = 0.0499) and fewer are down-modulated (14.3% against 17.0%, p = 0.0062), by chi-squared tests.
outcomes.source: Results, Spatiotemporal dynamics of neocortical activity, paragraph 4; Figure 3c
outcomes.quote: The fraction of up-modulated neurons was slightly but significantly higher in wM2 (16.0%) than in ALM (14.2%) ( p = 0.0499, chi-squared test), whereas the fraction of down-modulated neurons was significantly lower in wM2 (14.3 %) compared to ALM (17.0 %) ( p = 0.0062, chi-squared test).

statistics.test: chi-squared test
chi-squared test

outcomes.notes: Under the Methods' quiet rule (seed 5 given as measured; seeds 5 to 7) up-modulated wM2 13.6 to 13.8% against ALM 11.6 to 11.8% (chi-squared p 0.020 to 0.037) and down-modulated 10.9 to 11.1% against 13.6 to 14.0% (p 0.0006 to 0.0046); both directions and both tests hold, but all four fractions are below tolerance. With the code's mean absolute deviation the fractions are the paper's (up 16.0 to 16.3% against 14.3%, down 14.0 to 14.3% against 17.0%), with up-modulation p 0.047 to 0.077 by seed (paper 0.0499) and down-modulation p 0.002 to 0.005.
deviations: Windows are the code's bins 181:200 and 81:100 (Modulation.m), 0.8 to 1.0 s against -0.2 to 0 s.
Units are CCF-filtered (header convention); Modulation.m itself applies no CCF filter.

outcomes.statement: During the late delay of Go-tone Whisker trials, wM2 infragranular neurons change their firing more than supragranular neurons (1.2 +/- 0.1 Hz against 0.03 +/- 0.10 Hz, p = 1.7 x 10^-7, two-sample t-test), while no layer difference is detected in A1, wS2 or ALM.
outcomes.source: Results, Spatiotemporal dynamics of neocortical activity, paragraph 5; Figure 3d
outcomes.quote: Statistical tests indicated that neuronal activity during the late delay period of Go-tone trials differed significantly across cortical layers in wM2, with infragranular neurons having larger changes in firing rates than supragranular neurons (1.2 ± 0.1 Hz vs 0.03 ± 0.10 Hz; two-sample t-test, p = 1.7 × 10⁻⁷), whereas no significant differences were detected in A1, wS2, or ALM.

statistics.test: two-sample t-test

outcomes.notes: wM2 infragranular 0.955 +/- 0.119 Hz (2,046 neurons) against supragranular -0.055 +/- 0.093 Hz (703), t-test p 1.56e-06; the supragranular value is within tolerance, the infragranular below it (1.1 to 1.3). No layer pair differs in A1, wS2 or ALM (smallest p 0.21). The criterion's partial case (wM2 holds, one other pair significant) does not fit this result; it is recorded as partial because the effect and the absence elsewhere hold and one value is low. With the code's mean absolute deviation the wM2 values are 1.128 and -0.003 Hz (p 2.04e-07), within tolerance.
deviations: The criterion's partial case (wM2 holds and one other layer pair is significant) does not cover a wM2 value below tolerance with no other pair significant. Partial is assumed as the nearest case, since the effect, its significance and its absence elsewhere hold and one of the two wM2 values is low; this is the author's judgement, not the criterion's.

outcomes.statement: The paper's cluster labels (processed_data/Data_Clustering.mat on Zenodo) can be matched to the dataset's units, so that claims about named clusters can be tested on the dataset.
outcomes.source: Data availability and Code availability; Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.17973874, processed_data/Data_Clustering.mat and processed_data_code/psth_10ms.m
outcomes.notes: All 10,294 labelled neurons map by the rebuilt global index (13,793 units in the dataset) to distinct dataset units with the same probe area, CCF label and layer, and each is one of the 10,294 units analysed here.

outcomes.statement: Clustering all 10,294 neurons on their average activity in the five correct trial types (PCA, spectral embedding, Gaussian mixture model) gives 29 clusters at the minimum of the Bayesian Information Criterion.
outcomes.source: Results, Spatiotemporal dynamics of neocortical activity, paragraph 6; Figure 4a; Methods, Clustering of neuronal responses
outcomes.quote: The BIC analysis indicated that 29 clusters provided the best trade-off between accuracy and parsimony.
outcomes.notes: Following the Methods (10 ms PSTHs of the five correct types, 10,292 neurons with a nonzero range, 17 PCs, Gaussian similarity with sigma 0.0455 for a mean similarity of 0.5, eigenvectors 2 to 17, diagonal GMM with the code's reg_covar 0) the BIC minimum is at k = 36, 40, 42 and 42 for four seeds of 5 initialisations and at k = 40 for the best of the 20, outside the 20 to 38 band; k = 29 is 741 units above the minimum and the BIC over k = 30 to 44 spans 784 units. One seed alone (k = 36) would give partial, so the outcome rests on the pooled initialisations and is not stable. The code's variant (100 ms bins, whisker-only quiet rule, exp(-d/0.07975), mean similarity 0.500) gives k = 33 and 35 by seed and 33 for the best of 10. The first run (reg_covar 1e-6, 5 initialisations) gave k = 44 and 36.
deviations: 5 GMM initialisations per k and seed (4 seeds, 20 in all; code variant 2 seeds) in place of the code's 1,000 (time). This is an assumption, that the best of 20 initialisations stands for the best of 1,000; more initialisations can only lower the BIC at each k, so the minimum could move.

Row centring, unscaled left singular vectors, eigenvectors 2 to 17, the k grid, diagonal covariance and reg_covar 0 are the code's (Data_Clustering.ipynb, A4_spectral_embedding and A6_GMM_grid_search, lines printed in the notebook).
The shuffle rule for the number of PCs (1,000 shuffled PCAs) is not run; 17 PCs as the Methods.
Sessions with fewer than 3 quiet trials of a correct type would be skipped (code); none were.

outcomes.statement: Some clusters represent sensory responses (cluster 1, fast auditory response, mostly A1 neurons; cluster 29, fast whisker response, mostly wS1 and wS2), clusters 11 and 25 fire during the delay only on Go-tone trials and consist mainly of wM2 and ALM neurons, and cluster 4 decreases its firing during the Go-tone delay and is spread over the five areas.
outcomes.source: Results, Spatiotemporal dynamics of neocortical activity, paragraph 7; Figure 4a-b
outcomes.quote: Cluster #1 had a large and fast response to the auditory cue and mostly consisted of neurons in A1, whereas Cluster #29 responded strongly and rapidly to whisker deflection and mostly consisted of neurons in wS1 and wS2. A few clusters showed strong context-dependent firing selectivity comparing Go-tone and Nogo-tone trials, most notably Clusters #11 and #25, which showed prominent delay period firing only in Go-tone trials and mainly consisted of neurons in wM2 and ALM ( Fig. 4b ). Interestingly, another cluster, Cluster #4, showed a prominent decrease in firing rate during the delay period selectively for Go-tone trials and neurons in this cluster were widely distributed across the five recorded cortical areas
outcomes.notes: The readings of "mostly" give different outcomes. Cluster 1 (187 neurons) has a fast auditory response (13.0 to 17.3 Hz over 0 to 30 ms) and its largest share in A1 (30.5%; wS2 21.4%, wS1 20.3%) but not more than half, so reading (b) gives reproduced and reading (a) partially reproduced. The other parts hold under both readings; cluster 29 is 45.2% wS1 and 41.5% wS2 with a 21.7 to 21.9 Hz whisker response; clusters 11 and 25 are 90.4% and 83.1% wM2 and ALM and fire more in Hit than Nogo CR trials over the late delay (11.54 against -0.79 Hz, 3.56 against -0.29 Hz); cluster 4 fires less in Hit (-1.60 against 0.05 Hz) and has 7.1 to 31.9% of its neurons in each area. The question of what "mostly" means is for the paper's authors (findings).
deviations: The response of clusters 1 and 29 is shown for each correct trial type that has the stimulus; the criterion does not say which trials.

outcomes.statement: Comparing Hit with Nogo-tone Whisker correct rejection trials in the last 200 ms of the delay, wM2 and ALM have the highest proportions of context-modulated neurons (wM2, 20% increase firing by 8 Hz on average, 14% decrease by 3 Hz; ALM, 17% increase by 8 Hz, 16% decrease by 3 Hz), and wM2 has the largest proportion of Go-tone excited neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding context from neuronal activity during the delay period, paragraph 1; Figure 5a
outcomes.quote: Overall, we found the highest proportion of significantly modulated neurons in wM2 (20% of neurons increased firing on average by 8 Hz and 14% decreased firing by 3 Hz) and ALM (17% increased firing by 8 Hz and 16% decreased firing by 3 Hz). Thus, wM2 contained the largest proportion of Go-tone excited neurons during the delay period.
outcomes.notes: Under the Methods' quiet rule the wM2 up-modulated fraction is the largest of the five areas (17.86%) and wM2 (29.4%) and ALM (27.4%) have more modulated neurons than A1, wS1 and wS2 (at most 15.5%); the four firing changes are within tolerance but the four fractions are below it (4 of 8 values). With the code's mean absolute deviation all eight are within tolerance (wM2 20.04%, 8.14 Hz, 14.11%, -2.77 Hz; ALM 16.72%, 7.53 Hz, 16.14%, -2.97 Hz).

outcomes.statement: With 50 neurons per area, context (Hit against Nogo-tone Whisker CR) is decoded in the last 200 ms of the delay above baseline in every area, but far better in wM2 (64 +/- 1%) and ALM (61 +/- 1%) than in A1 (52 +/- 1%), wS1 (52 +/- 1%) and wS2 (52 +/- 0.4%).
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding context from neuronal activity during the delay period, paragraph 2; Figure 5b
outcomes.quote: Focusing on the last 200 ms of the delay period, during which orofacial movements are absent, the auditory context could be decoded from the firing of 50 neurons in each area with accuracy varying across cortical regions: i) A1, 52 ± 1%, p = 0.008, n = 8 sessions across N = 6 mice; ii) wS1, 52 ± 1%, p = 0.0003, n = 17 sessions across N = 9 mice; iii) wS2, 52 ± 0.4%, p = 0.0003, n = 19 sessions across N = 9 mice; iv) wM2, 64 ± 1%, p = 0.0002, n = 18 sessions across N = 8 mice; and v) ALM, 61 ± 1%, p = 0.0004, n = 16 sessions across N = 6 mice.

Code's nu-SVC (reading b, listed as measured) A1 52.6, wS1 51.9, wS2 51.4, wM2 62.0, ALM 58.9% (2 of 5 within tolerance); Methods' grid search (reading a) 53.1, 52.3, 52.0, 63.1 and 58.5% (3 of 5). Every area is above baseline (Wilcoxon p 0.0078 or less with the code's decoder, 0.027 or less with the grid search; baseline 49.98 to 50.09%) and wM2 and ALM exceed A1, wS1 and wS2 under both readings. Sessions with at least 50 neurons are the paper's (8, 17, 19, 18, 16). Five seed sets of 5 subsets move the code decoder's area means by at most 1.02 points (wM2 61.7 to 62.7, ALM 58.8 to 59.5%), each with 2 of 5 within tolerance. With the code's quiet rule (mean absolute deviation, code's decoder only) 52.5, 52.2, 51.5, 62.9 and 61.6% (3 of 5 within; ALM within, wM2 1.1 points low), all tests p < 0.05, ordering holds, also partial.
deviations: 5 random subsets of 50 neurons per session (code's decoder; four more seed sets on the delay bins) and 1 subset on every 5th baseline bin (grid search), in place of 100 subsets; the run times printed in this run put 100 subsets at about 53 min for the code's decoder and 44 h for the grid search.
The grid search is not run with the code's quiet rule (time).
The grid for the Methods' search (C from 10^-3 to 10^3 in decades) is the claims file's; the SVM caps libsvm iterations at 10^5.
sklearn's libsvm (NuSVC, SVC) stands in for the MATLAB libsvm interface; undersampling and folds draw their own random numbers.

outcomes.statement: Context decoding is at chance in the baseline, highest in A1 right after the cue, and during the delay falls in A1, wS1 and wS2 but rises in wM2 and ALM; with fewer neurons accuracy drops but wM2 and ALM stay above A1, wS1 and wS2.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding context from neuronal activity during the delay period, paragraph 2; Figure 5b left and right
outcomes.quote: Decoding in the baseline period was at chance level (50%) for all cortical regions, as expected. Immediately, upon presentation of the auditory contextual cue, the decoding of Go vs Nogo trials was highest in A1, but context could also be decoded from all other recorded cortical regions. The ability to decode context during the delay period rapidly decreased in A1, wS1 and wS2, but increased for wM2 and ALM. ... Decreasing the number of neurons per cortical region through further subsampling reduced decoding accuracy but maintained the overall conclusion that wM2 and ALM more strongly encode context compared to A1, wS1 and wS2.
outcomes.notes: With 50 neurons and the code's decoder (1) baseline accuracy is 49.98 to 50.09% in every area; (2) the cue accuracy is highest in A1 under both cue windows (70.3% over 0 to 30 ms, 65.6% over 0 to 200 ms; at most 57.4 and 57.9% elsewhere); (3) delay accuracy falls below the cue accuracy in A1, wS1 and wS2 and rises above it in wM2 and ALM under both windows; (4) wM2 and ALM exceed A1, wS1 and wS2 at every count from 5 to 50 neurons (at 5 by 0.47 to 0.51 points). The Methods' grid search (one subset) gives the same for all four parts, (1) baseline 48.5 to 50.3%, (2) A1 highest (68.4% and 65.0%; at most 57.4% elsewhere), (3) in all five areas under both windows, (4) at 5, 25 and 50 neurons.
deviations: 3 subsets per session for 5 to 45 neurons (paper 100); the grid search is run with one subset, at 5, 25 and 50 neurons only.

outcomes.statement: Removing cluster 11 reduces late-delay context decoding in wM2 (by 3.8 +/- 1.0%) and ALM (4.5 +/- 1.4%) with no significant effect in A1, wS1 and wS2; removing cluster 25 also reduces it in wM2 (1.6 +/- 0.6%) and ALM (2.0 +/- 0.6%); removing any other cluster does not significantly decrease decoding.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding context from neuronal activity during the delay period, paragraph 3; Figure 5c
outcomes.quote: Removal of Cluster #11 reduced decoding accuracy by 3.8 ± 1.0% ( p = 0.008) for wM2 and by 4.5 ± 1.4% ( p = 0.008) for ALM, with no significant effect upon A1, wS1 and wS2. Removal of Cluster #25 also reduced significantly the decoding accuracy by 1.6 ± 0.6% ( p = 0.03) for wM2 and by 2.0 ± 0.6% ( p = 0.03) for ALM.

outcomes.notes: Both readings give not reproduced, so the criterion's block for readings that disagree does not apply. Methods' grid search (one run, clusters 11 and 25 only), cluster 11 lowers wM2 by 4.17 and ALM by 4.73 points (significant) but also wS1 by 0.20 (FDR p 0.030), and cluster 25's 1.31 and 1.92 points are not significant (FDR p 0.085), so not reproduced. Code's nu-SVC, seed set 0, cluster 11 lowers delay decoding in wM2 by 4.61 +/- 0.89 and ALM by 4.45 +/- 1.20 points (FDR p 0.0009 and 0.0002) and not significantly in A1, wS1, wS2; cluster 25 by 1.30 +/- 0.53 and 1.70 +/- 0.57 (FDR p 0.048 both); all four within tolerance; one other pair is significant (cluster 24 in A1, 0.49 points, p 0.029), so partially reproduced. In seed sets 1 and 2 cluster 25 is not significant (FDR p 0.075 to 0.234), and the mean of the three sets has the four values within tolerance and significant but three other pairs significant (cluster 2 in wM2, cluster 13 in wM2 and ALM), so not reproduced; with the code's quiet rule cluster 11 is also significant in wS2, which the claim excludes (and cluster 26 in wM2), so not reproduced. Seed set 0 is the only run that gives partial; it was the first run, not a chosen main run. The claim depends on fig4b-named-clusters, which is blocked on what "mostly" means for cluster 1; this claim uses fig4b only for its cluster labels, which link fully (cluster-label-link), and fig4b's parts on clusters 11 and 25 hold under both readings (shares in wM2 and ALM 90.4% and 83.1%), so the third verification round judged that the dependency does not apply. Confidence is moderate, since the Methods' reading is one run for two clusters; testing the other 27 clusters could only add failures. The outcome was blocked (methods_underspecified) until the third verification round, which agreed with the change.
deviations: The decrease is with minus without the cluster (the criterion's without minus with, sign turned). The two decodings share their random state.
The grid search was run once, for clusters 11 and 25 only (all 29 would take about 40 min per run by the time this run printed).
The code's decoder was run in three seed sets and with the code's quiet rule.

outcomes.statement: In the first two PCs, A1, wS1 and wS2 activity returns near its start by the end of the delay, while in correct Go-tone trials wM2 and ALM settle within about 200 ms into a state far from the origin, reached with and without the whisker stimulus; Nogo correct rejections return to baseline and Miss trials fail to reach the Go-tone state. PC1 explains 11% (A1, wS1, wS2), 17% (wM2) and 14% (ALM) of variance, PC2 6% (A1, wS1, wS2) and 8% (wM2, ALM).
outcomes.source: Results, Context-dependent neuronal dynamics during the delay period, paragraph 1; Figure 6a
outcomes.quote: Neuronal activity in each cortical area exhibited a rapid response after tone onset in PC1 (explained variance: A1, 11%; wS1, 11%; wS2, 11%; wM2, 17%; and ALM 14%) and PC2 (explained variance: A1, 6%; wS1, 6%; wS2, 6%; wM2, 8%; and ALM 8%). Activity in A1, wS1 and wS2 followed an apparently cyclic trajectory, returning near to the start point by the end of the delay period. However, in correct Go-tone trials, neuronal activity in wM2 and ALM settled rapidly (within ~200 ms) into an apparent fixed point far from the origin ... Interestingly, in error trials where the mouse did not lick in response to the whisker stimulus preceded by a Go-tone (i.e., Miss trials), the neural activity in wM2 and ALM failed to reach the apparent attractor state of correct Go-tone trials.
outcomes.notes: The geometry holds; end-of-delay distances from baseline in wM2 Hit 7.14 and Go-tone No-Whisker 5.87 against Nogo CR 0.96 and Miss 1.90; in ALM 6.64 and 5.65 against 0.45 and 1.95; in A1, wS1 and wS2 the Hit trajectory is at 0.05 to 0.16 of its maximum distance at 1.0 s. Seven of ten explained variances are within tolerance (PC1 wS1 9.77 and wM2 14.97, PC2 ALM 6.79 below). With the code's mean absolute deviation all ten are within tolerance (PC1 11.1, 10.6, 11.5, 16.6, 14.3; PC2 6.0, 6.1, 6.2, 8.2, 7.8). The legend's reading (PCs on Hit and Nogo CR) gives PC1 16.7 to 27.2%.
deviations: The distance measures and the half-maximum rule are the claims file's (marked open in its check).
Neurons with no trials of a condition (NaN) or no range are dropped (133 wM2, 101 ALM, 3 wS2), as the code's normalisation does.

outcomes.source: Results, Context-dependent neuronal dynamics during the delay period, paragraph 2; Figure 6b
outcomes.quote: Activity in the context coding dimension was high in wM2 and ALM throughout the delay period in correct Go-tone Hit trials, but strongly reduced in the incorrect Go-tone Miss trials.

outcomes.statement: In wM2 and ALM the Go-tone induces a long-lasting increase in correlated population activity during the delay in Hit and Go-tone No-Whisker trials, absent in Nogo-tone and Miss trials, while in A1, wS1 and wS2 the cue evokes only a brief increase.
outcomes.source: Results, Context-dependent neuronal dynamics during the delay period, paragraph 3; Figure 6c
outcomes.quote: Presentation of the auditory cue evoked a brief increase in correlated neuronal activity in A1, wS1 and wS2. However, in wM2 and ALM, the Go-tone induced a long-lasting increase in correlated neuronal activity during the delay period in both Hit and Go-tone No-Whisker Correct Rejection trials. In contrast, presentation of the Nogo-tone failed to induce network states with high temporal correlation. Importantly, the highly-correlated network state during the delay period was also absent in Miss trials

outcomes.source: Results, Context-dependent processing of the whisker stimulus, paragraph 1; Figure 7b
outcomes.quote: we found significant changes in evoked activity, with an early transient reduction in the whisker response in wS1 and wS2 for Go-tone trials, followed by an overall increased activity in most cortical regions at later times
outcomes.notes: FDR within each area; wS1 has significant negative Hit minus CR bins at 1.015 and 1.020 s and wS2 at 1.010 to 1.025 s; all five areas have significant positive bins from 1.030 s on (ALM from 1.030, wM2 1.035, wS1 and wS2 1.040, A1 1.065 s). The code's FDR over all areas and bins gives the same bins for wS1, wM2 and ALM, and for wS2 after the stimulus; wS2's pre-stimulus negative bins (0.96 and 0.965 s, FDR within the area) the one at 0.96 s drops out under it.

outcomes.statement: Activity projected on a whisker coding direction, defined from the first 30 ms of No-tone Whisker responses, shows no significant difference between Go-tone and Nogo-tone contexts.
outcomes.source: Results, Context-dependent processing of the whisker stimulus, paragraph 1; Figure 7c
outcomes.quote: However, no significant context differences were found in analyses of a whisker sensory response coding direction based on the 30 ms of activity evoked by whisker stimuli without a preceding tone cue and without subsequent licking
outcomes.notes: Claim of absence, judged by the code's Kruskal-Wallis test; no area differs (p 0.31 to 0.97; variants smallest p 0.19). Hit minus Nogo CR projections -0.022 to 0.061. The paired Wilcoxon test, not the paper's, gives wS2 p 0.096 in the main run and below 0.05 in wS2 and A1 in some variants.

30% training trials, as Coding_direction_5ms.m.

outcomes.statement: Decoding context from baseline-subtracted activity in 5 ms bins after the whisker stimulus, significant decoding appears transiently in A1 and wS2 at 15 ms for one bin, and persistently in wM2 from 20 ms and in ALM from 25 ms after the stimulus.
outcomes.source: Results, Context-dependent processing of the whisker stimulus, paragraph 2; Figure 7d
outcomes.quote: we found that significant context-dependent sensory processing transiently appeared in A1 and wS2 at 15 ms after whisker stimulus for a single 5 ms-time bin; and appeared in a more lasting manner in wM2 at 20 ms after whisker stimulus (and all later time bins) and in ALM at 25 ms after whisker stimulus (and all later times)
outcomes.notes: The two SVM readings give different outcomes. Code's nu-SVC (5 runs, as the code, 10 baseline bins) gives persistent decoding from 1.020 s in wM2 and 1.025 s in ALM and only from 1.085, 1.060 and 1.060 s in A1, wS1 and wS2, so the criterion holds; A1 has a single significant bin at 1.015 s, as the paper reports. (The first run, with 1 run, gave 1.025 and 1.035 s.) The Methods' grid search (1 run, 2 baseline bins) gives wM2 from 1.040 s and ALM from 1.035 s, so wM2 does not precede ALM and the claim is not reproduced. Neither reading shows a single significant bin at 15 ms in wS2 (wS2 has an isolated bin at 1.020 s with the grid search). The Methods' onsets are one bin apart, on a reduced run (2 of 10 baseline bins, 1 run), so this reading is weak, as the verifier's second round says.
deviations: The grid search uses 1 run and 2 of the 10 baseline bins; all 10 would take about 58 min per run by the time this run printed (30 min in the run the verifier read). A run with all 10 bins, in a notebook of its own, was started for this revision and had not finished after 53 min, when the runner's two-hour limit on one command stopped the entry's run; it was dropped, so the Methods' result still rests on 2 bins and one run.

outcomes.statement: In the first 30 ms after the whisker stimulus, only wM2 activity diverges into separate states for lick and no-lick trials, mainly along the context coding direction, and at 30 ms distinguishes lick from no-lick trials both in correct Go-tone and error Nogo-tone conditions; ALM shows a weaker effect and A1, wS1 and wS2 none.
outcomes.source: Results, Context-dependent processing of the whisker stimulus, paragraph 3; Figure 8a
outcomes.quote: Only wM2 showed a clear divergence of trajectories into two distinct states corresponding to lick vs no-lick outcomes. This separation was primarily along the context coding direction. Single-session analyses confirmed that wM2 activity at 30 ms significantly distinguished lick from no-lick trials both in correct Go-tone and error Nogo-tone conditions ( Supplementary Fig. 17 ). ALM showed a weaker effect, and no significant differences were observed in A1, wS1, or wS2.
outcomes.notes: In wM2 the six groups differ (Kruskal-Wallis p 0.0048) and Go-tone lick trials are above Go-tone no-lick trials (LSD p 0.0041), but Nogo-tone lick (false alarm) trials are not above Nogo-tone no-lick trials (p 0.28; variants 0.08 to 0.36), so wM2 holds for one context, the criterion's partial case. A1, wS1 and wS2 show no significant lick against no-lick comparison (p 0.40 or more). ALM Kruskal-Wallis p below 0.0001, Go-tone p 0.0008, Nogo-tone p 0.028. The Supplementary Fig. 17 legend gives wM2's Nogo-tone result as "Nogo-tone Lick vs No tone no lick trials" (p 0.04); that pair gives p 0.22 in wM2 (variants 0.09 to 0.37), also not significant; whether the criterion's pair is the paper's is asked of a reader (questions/ghaderi-2026.yaml).
deviations: As fig7c, the context direction at 5 ms is built from the 10 ms counts.

outcomes.statement: At 30 ms after the whisker stimulus, activity along a lick coding direction defined from spontaneous licking separates lick from no-lick trials in wM2 for Go-tone, Nogo-tone (false alarm) and No-tone trials, in ALM only for correct trials, and not in A1, wS1 or wS2.
outcomes.source: Results, Context-dependent processing of the whisker stimulus, paragraph 4; Figure 8b
outcomes.quote: Projecting neuronal activity in the lick coding direction revealed separation between lick and no-lick trials for both correct and false alarm cases in wM2 at 30 ms after delivery of the whisker stimulus ( Fig. 8b ). The lick coding direction did not separate between lick and no-lick trials in A1, wS1 or wS2 at this early time point. Neuronal activity in ALM was higher in the lick coding direction only for correct trials, but false alarm lick trials were not different from no-lick trials at 30 ms post whisker stimulus time.

outcomes.notes: At 1.2 to 1.4 s ALM, wM2, wS2 and wS1 each give Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.05 (0.0002, below 0.0001, below 0.0001, 0.0076) with lick groups significantly above no-lick groups and A1 does not (p 0.40), but under both readings wM2, not ALM, has the largest effect (Cohen's d wM2 3.80, ALM 1.95, wS2 1.16, wS1 0.94; Kruskal-Wallis statistic wM2 49.2, wS2 27.3, ALM 24.5, wS1 15.8). The readings agree on the largest area, so the claim fails on its ranking. The plain difference of mean projections, not a criterion reading, ranks ALM 0.46, wM2 0.35, wS2 0.18, wS1 0.11, the paper's order. The Supplementary Fig. 18 legend, which the claims file did not read, says "The projection amplitude in the lick coding direction was largest for ALM, followed by wM2, wS2 and wS1 (in rank order), with A1 having the smallest and not significant difference", which reads as that difference; under it the claim would be reproduced. findings.statement: The Methods define quiet trials with the median absolute deviation; the code (nwb_findQuietTrial.m) calls MATLAB mad() with its default, the mean absolute deviation, which keeps more trials (60% against 45% of completed trials). With the code's rule the single-neuron fractions of Fig. 3c and 5a, the layer values of Fig. 3d and the explained variances of Fig. 6a come out at the paper's values; with the Methods' rule they are lower. The paper's numbers appear to come from the code's rule.

The dandiset gives each unit a probe location and an Allen CCF label but not which CCF labels make up the paper's five areas. Only with data_helpers/Area_list.mat from the Zenodo record do the unit counts match the paper (10,294); without it 12,066 units sit on the five areas' probes.

In 12 optogenetic sessions (11 of mouse PG061 and one of PG021) the subject genotype is C57BL/6JRj, which carries no ChR2, although the paper inactivates VGAT-ChR2 mice and light trials in these sessions reduce licking as in the others; the other sessions of PG021 give VGAT_ChR2-eYFP.

The units' spike_width is described as "Trough to peak in ms" but holds seconds (0.0001 to 0.0012); times 1000 the RS and FS flags fit the Methods' thresholds (RS 0.467 to 1.200 ms, FS 0.100 to 0.333 ms).

Several trial-table descriptions do not fit their columns, for example opto_area ("laser light duration", holds an area name), opto_stim_start_time ("Pulse duration in s"), opto_stim_stop_time ("Individual pulse timestamps") and context ("Boolean for sound", holds go_tone, nogo_tone or no_tone).

Eleven trials of sub-PG028_ses-20210318T163504 have trial_type 0, outside the five types, and sub-PG076_ses-20220502T140636 has no No-tone trials. 343 trials have no video frames in their -1 to 2 s window, at least one in every session and most in sub-PG061_ses-20220212T233813 (243) and sub-PG038_ses-20210316T152753 (29), so they cannot be classed as quiet. sub-PG038_ses-20210317T180556 has no unit that passes the CCF filter.

The Fig. 2 legend gives mean +/- SD and 1,000 bootstrap iterations; the reported spreads match the SEM over sessions (A1 Auditory 4.1 against SD 16.9) and the reported p-values (0.0003, 0.0004) are reached with the code's 10,000 iterations, not with 1,000 (smallest 0.002 before FDR).
The Results and Fig. 1c give 35 recording sessions, which the dandiset holds; the Methods say 34. The Methods give 8 mice for ALM inactivation; the dandiset has ALM sessions from 7 mice.

Question for the authors on Fig. 4b. Does "mostly consisted of neurons in A1" for cluster 1 mean more than half of its neurons or the largest share of any area? With the paper's labels cluster 1 is 30.5% A1, 21.4% wS2 and 20.3% wS1, so the claim holds under the second reading only.

Question for the authors on the population decoders (Fig. 5b to 5d, 7d). The Methods say SVM parameters were chosen by grid search with nested cross-validation but give no grid; the code trains libsvm nu-SVC with default parameters and no search. Which was used, and over which grid? With a C grid of 10^-3 to 10^3 the cluster-removal and post-whisker results differ from the code's decoder (Fig. 5c cluster 25 not significant; Fig. 7d wM2 onset after ALM).

Question for the authors on Fig. 1f. How is "time to 20% max" computed, on the session-mean trace or on each trial, and over which window is the maximum taken? None of the code computes it. With the maximum over the 1 s response window the session-mean reading gives 54.4, 115.3 and 192.4 ms and the per-trial reading 94.6, 142.9 and 254.6 ms, against the reported 58, 115 and 231 ms; with the maximum over the plotted 1.0 to 1.2 s the tongue latency cannot reach 231 ms.

The detected lick times and lick mask used for the lick coding direction (Fig. 8b, Supplementary Fig. 18) are only in the Zenodo record (Lick_times.mat); the dandiset holds the raw piezo lick trace and the jaw trace, and its BehavioralEvents hold only Valve_OpeningTime in all 35 sessions (printed in reproduce_ghaderi_2026.ipynb, fig8b-lick-coding-direction).

entries.name: ghaderi-2026
entries.title: Contextual gating of whisker responses by frontal cortex (Ghaderi et al. 2026)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Ghaderi, Crochet and Petersen (2026) on dandiset 001530, which holds 35 Neuropixels sessions in 14 mice performing a delayed context-dependent whisker detection task and 91 optogenetic inactivation sessions. It compares lick probabilities, the effect of inactivating six cortical areas in three task epochs, unit counts, single-neuron and population activity in five areas, context decoding during the delay and after the whisker stimulus, and the clustering of neuronal responses.
